newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch property firm Bouwfonds to let outsiders in.
newsitem.headline: Dutch property firm Bouwfonds to let outsiders in.

text.p: Dutch property developer and financing group Bouwfonds Nederlandse Gemeenten said on Thursday it would allow non-municipal shareholders in a few years' time.
Bouwfonds, now owned by 572 local Dutch towns, will change its articles of association to enable other shareholders to step in, chairman John Simons told a news conference.

The group, one of the largest players in the Dutch housing and mortgage markets, had planned to privately place new shares worth 175 million guilders with Dutch institutional investors, but 15 percent of the present shareholders wanted to increase their stakes and will take up all of the issue.

Simons said this had postponed institutional investors from taking stakes in Bouwfonds by two or three years, but the need for a broader shareholder base remained to cover future financing requirements. In the even longer term, Bouwfonds might seek a bourse listing, he added.

Bouwfonds earlier posted a 1996 net profit from ordinary operations of 121 million guilders, up from 108 million in 1995. About two-thirds of its income is generated by mortgages and project financing and the other third by property development.
Simons said property development income was seen growing to about 40 percent of group income within five years.
For 1997, a profit rise of at least 15 percent is envisaged and in later years Bouwfonds aims at posting annual profit growth of at least 10 percent.
It now has a mortgage portfolio of 23.3 billion guilders and 1996 production of new mortgage loans totalled 4.2 billion.
The group expected the demand for Dutch houses to remain high in 1997 but added it does not see mortgage production equalling last year's record levels.
Many of these loans actually consisted of refinancing previous arrangements at cheaper conditions by private clients and there are not many left who can still do so, Simons said.
Bouwfonds started expanding internationally in recent years, by setting up housing projects in Germany and building offices and houses in Belgium.
Simons said these activities were still rather modest but its presence in Germany had also opened the way to raise funding in that country.

In 1996, the group borrowed four billion guilders in the private placement markets. About 70 percent of this was lent by the 20 largest Dutch financial institutions, including Bank voor Nederlandse Gemeenten (BNG), Simons said.
